html:
The Edicts of Ashoka are over thirty inscriptions that the Maurya emperor Ashoka had carved on rocks, cave walls and polished stone pillars across his empire, during his reign of about 268 to 232 BCE. They are the oldest Indian texts that can be dated with confidence.

Most are in Prakrit, a spoken language, in the Brahmi script; in the northwest some use Kharosthi, and near Kandahar there are versions in Greek and Aramaic. In them Ashoka speaks in the first person.

  • He tells of his remorse after the bloody Kalinga War.
  • He preaches dhamma: respect for parents and elders, kindness to servants and animals, honesty and tolerance among sects.
  • He limits animal sacrifice and the killing of animals for his kitchen.
  • He names Greek kings to whom he sent envoys, and the hospitals and wells he provided.

The script was forgotten later. In 1837 James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi, and Ashoka, until then a figure of Buddhist legend, became a historical ruler. Famous pillars include the Lion Capital at Sarnath and the pillar at Lumbini.
